title: Can every polynomial-time decision problem be efficiently parallelized?
formal: Is P=NC, where NC consists of decision languages recognized by logspace-uniform Boolean circuit families of polynomial size and polylogarithmic depth? Equivalently, does the Circuit Value Problem have such a circuit family?
definitions: P is deterministic polynomial time on ordinary Turing machines. For L∈NC there must be fixed constants c,k,C and a family (Cₙ)ₙ≥0 such that Cₙ decides membership in L correctly on every n-bit input, has at most C(n+2)ᶜ gates, and has depth at most C(log₂(n+2))ᵏ. Gates are two-input AND and OR and one-input NOT; fan-out is unrestricted and one output bit is designated. Depth is the longest input-to-output gate path. A deterministic O(log(n+2))-space transducer given 1ⁿ must output the description of Cₙ; its polynomial output bound is part of the size requirement. Constants and the generator may depend on L but not on n. Circuit Value receives an explicit topologically ordered Boolean gate DAG, its input-bit values, and an output-gate index; it asks whether that gate evaluates to 1. Its input length n is the entire binary encoding length, and malformed encodings are rejected. No randomization, advice, oracle, or restriction to monotone gates is permitted.
answer_criterion: Answer yes by constructing the stated uniform polynomial-size, polylogarithmic-depth circuits for Circuit Value, or by proving P⊆NC another way. Answer no by exhibiting a language in P outside NC, ruling out every fixed polylogarithmic depth exponent and every polynomial size bound for that language. A lower bound for a single evaluation strategy or for circuits without NOT gates is insufficient.
context:
Circuit evaluation makes the apparent obstacle concrete. A sequential algorithm processes the gates in their supplied topological order and computes every value in polynomial time. A circuit can contain a long chain of dependent gates, but that chain only limits the obvious evaluation procedure. A faster algorithm may reorganize the computation, exploit algebraic identities, or avoid evaluating intermediate gates. Proving that every possible efficient parallel computation must retain substantial sequential dependence is the unresolved step.

Ladner proved Circuit Value complete for P under logarithmic-space reductions. These reductions themselves admit NC computation, and NC is closed under their composition. An NC algorithm for this one problem would therefore parallelize every problem in P. P-completeness supplies this conditional consequence; it does not already prove the absence of a parallel algorithm.

The resource tradeoff is polynomial total circuit size against polylogarithmic dependency depth. The exponent of the polynomial work budget may be large, so a positive answer would not automatically provide nearly linear work or useful speedups on a small machine. Logspace uniformity prevents the circuit descriptions from supplying arbitrary nonuniform information. The union over all fixed depth exponents also makes this broader than asking whether P equals NC¹.

Restricted circuit models reveal real obstructions. Raz and McKenzie separate monotone NC from monotone P, and separate consecutive levels of the monotone NC hierarchy. Their lower bounds restrict the computing circuit to AND and OR. A monotone function can still have a substantially more powerful circuit when NOT gates are allowed, so the restriction cannot be removed from the conclusion.

Recent matching lower bounds sharpen this caution. Cavalar and coauthors prove a stretched-exponential monotone circuit-size lower bound for perfect matching, a problem with polynomial-time general algorithms. The separation measures the cost of forbidding negation. It supplies progress in circuit lower bounds while leaving the general uniform parallel-computation question untouched.
why: This asks whether a feasible computation can require intrinsically many sequential stages even when polynomially many processors are available. It is the central unresolved premise behind P-completeness as an explanation for resistance to parallelization, spanning graph algorithms, simulation, optimization, and language processing.

importance.reason: The foundational tractability question for parallel computation: whether every polynomial-time task admits polylogarithmic dependency depth with polynomial work.

progress.text: Ladner establishes that Circuit Value is logspace complete for P, giving a concrete universal target for efficient parallelization.
Greenlaw, Hoover, and Ruzzo organize the theory of P-completeness and its open P-versus-NC question, including uniform circuit and parallel-machine formulations.
Raz and McKenzie prove monotone NC≠monotone P and a strict monotone NC hierarchy. These results restrict the gates used by the computing circuits.

Cavalar and coauthors prove perfect matching requires monotone circuit size 2^{n^{Ω(1)}}, improving Razborov’s quasipolynomial lower bound. The November 2025 revision appears in STOC 2026; general Boolean circuits are not covered.

status_note: P versus NC is explicitly open in the primary P-completeness monograph. The literature check through 10 September 2026 located no unrestricted resolution. Monotone-circuit separations do not settle the stated Boolean circuit model.
